title: Why This Bird Sings at 2AM: 5 Animals Living With Our Noise
description: A robin singing at 2am, orcas that shout over boats, city birds with a new accent. We count down five animals dealing with human noise, ending with a new Science study of 177 species: in 8 out of 10 species, noise changed their bodies or behaviour, and noisy places held 37% fewer animals. Which one surprised you? Tell me in the comments. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.
tags: why do birds sing at night

scenes.hook: WHY IS THIS BIRD SINGING AT 2AM?
scenes.say: It's 2am, the street is dark, and a tiny bird is singing.

scenes.label: Not a nightingale
scenes.say: That's not a nightingale. It's a European robin. And it's awake because of you. Stay until the end, because number one explains it all.

scenes.label: Your noise
scenes.say: Okay, so here's the thing. You are a loud neighbour. Cars, buses, ships, leaf blowers. All of it.
And animals have to live right next door. Some of them are fighting back in ways that sound almost human.

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: Today we count down five animals dealing with your noise. Stay for number one.
Because number one isn't one animal. It's a brand new study of 177 species, published this month in Science.

scenes.label: Speaking up
scenes.say: Number five. Killer whales that raise their voices like you do at a loud party.
These are the Southern Resident orcas. They live in the busy waters around Seattle.

scenes.label: Busy water
scenes.say: Boats are everywhere there. Motors hum all day, and sound travels really far underwater.
Orcas talk with calls. They use them to stay together and to find each other in murky water.

scenes.label: Recorded
scenes.say: So scientists from NOAA dropped calibrated microphones in the water and measured two things.
How loud the background noise was. And how loud each whale call was.

scenes.label: +1 for +1
scenes.say: The result? For every one decibel the noise went up, the whales got one decibel louder.
One for one. Just like you, shouting a little more every time the music gets turned up.

scenes.label: Why it matters
scenes.say: Southern Residents are endangered. If a mother can't hear her calf over an engine, the family can drift apart.
And the more boats were nearby, the noisier the water got. Think about that next time you're on a ferry.

scenes.label: Louder, not quieter
scenes.say: Number four is a giant. The North Atlantic right whale, one of the most endangered whales on Earth.
Researchers put small sound tags on individual whales. Not on the boat. On the whale itself.
That way they could hear exactly what one whale said, and how loud the ocean was around it.

scenes.label: Same trick
scenes.say: And it did the same thing as the orcas. When the noise went up, it called louder.
But here's the twist. Shouting costs energy. And you can only shout so loud.

scenes.label: A hidden cost
scenes.say: The scientists also warned it changes how easy these whales are for us to find and protect with microphones.
So a whale that's already in trouble has to work harder just to be heard. That's number four.

scenes.label: Quick question
scenes.say: Okay, quick question for you. Could you keep shouting all day, every day, just to talk to your family?

scenes.label: Halfway there
scenes.say: So that's two ocean giants raising their voices. But you don't need to live in the sea to hear this happening.
It's happening right outside your window, maybe right now. And the next one has a city accent.

scenes.label: City accent
scenes.say: Number three is a bird you've probably heard without noticing. The great tit.
Its song sounds a bit like a squeaky bicycle pump. Tee-cha, tee-cha, tee-cha.

scenes.label: Leiden, 2003
scenes.say: In 2003, a Dutch researcher named Hans Slabbekoorn recorded great tits around the city of Leiden.
He measured the street noise too, before, during and after rush hour.

scenes.label: Higher notes
scenes.say: In the loudest spots, the birds sang with higher low notes. The deep part of the song was simply gone.

scenes.label: Engine rumble
scenes.say: Why? Engines rumble low. So the low notes were getting drowned out, like whispering next to a truck.
Later, his team compared ten big cities with ten nearby forests. London, Paris, Brussels, Prague.

scenes.label: Faster, higher
scenes.say: In every single pair, the city birds sang higher. And they sang in a hurry, with shorter notes.
Basically, city great tits have their own accent. Faster, higher, a bit stressed out. Sound familiar?

scenes.label: Not so simple
scenes.say: But here's the honest part. Other scientists ran the maths and found singing higher barely helps the sound travel.
Singing louder helps much more. So the high notes might just be a side effect of shouting.
Science is still arguing about it. Which, honestly, is the fun part.

scenes.label: Lab test
scenes.say: There is one more clue, though. In a lab, trained great tits found high songs easier to hear inside city noise.
In forest sounds, high and low songs were equally easy. So in the city, high notes may still give a small edge.

scenes.label: The night shift
scenes.say: Number two is our 2am singer. The European robin.
Robins sing to defend their patch. If a rival can't hear you, he walks right in, and you have to fight.

scenes.label: 121 spots
scenes.say: So scientists in Sheffield, England picked 121 places across the city, from quiet to really loud.
They visited every spot twice. Once in the day, once in the middle of the night.

scenes.label: 57 vs 49 dB
scenes.say: The city was louder by day, about 57 decibels on average. At night it dropped to around 49.

scenes.label: Night = quiet
scenes.say: And the robins that sang at night lived in the places that were noisiest during the day.

scenes.label: Not the lights
scenes.say: Everyone used to blame street lights for this. But the study found the light mattered much less than the daytime noise.

scenes.label: Same effort
scenes.say: And here's a cool detail. The night singers didn't sing less. They sang about as much as the daytime birds did.
So the robin just moved its concert to the night shift, when the traffic finally stops.
Imagine having to wait until 2am to finally talk to your neighbours. That's a robin's life in a busy city.

scenes.label: But wait
scenes.say: Okay. Whales shouting, birds changing their accent, robins on night shift. Is this just a few odd cases?
Or is it happening to almost every animal that lives near us, and we just never noticed?
That's exactly what two scientists in Belfast wanted to know. And the answer is our number one.

scenes.label: 177 species
scenes.say: Number one. Hansjoerg Kunc and Rouven Schmidt from Queen's University Belfast pulled together 214 experiments.
Those experiments covered 177 species, comparing animals in noise with animals in quiet.

scenes.label: 8 in 10
scenes.say: Their result came out this month in the journal Science. In 80 percent of the species, noise changed something.
Their bodies, their growth, or their behaviour. Stress hormones went up. Even stress inside their cells.

scenes.label: 37% fewer
scenes.say: And then the big one. For every 100 animals living in a quiet place, only about 63 lived in a noisy one.
That's 37 percent fewer animals, just because of the sound around them.

scenes.label: 2.5x the effort
scenes.say: Predators had it rough too. In noise they spent two and a half times more effort hunting.

scenes.label: 25% fewer catches
scenes.say: And they still caught about 25 percent fewer prey. Imagine working twice as hard and earning less.

scenes.label: Winners too
scenes.say: But not everyone loses. Prey animals got more nervous and watchful. And some predators actually win.
If noise scares prey out of hiding and into the open, a different hunter gets an easy meal.

scenes.label: Chain reaction
scenes.say: And that's the scary part. A change in one hunter ripples down to everything it eats, and everything that eats them.
So noise doesn't just bother animals. It quietly picks winners and losers, and reshapes whole communities.

scenes.label: Quiet zones
scenes.say: The fix the scientists point to sounds simple. Quiet zones. Places where animals can actually hear each other.

scenes.label: Library rules
scenes.say: Fewer engines near nests, quieter boats near whale families, less noise at the edges of parks and forests.
Think of it like a library for wildlife. And the good news? Unlike other pollution, sound stops the second we stop making it.

scenes.label: Recap
scenes.say: So, a quick recap. Orcas shout over boats. Right whales call louder. Great tits got a city accent.
Robins took the night shift. And across 177 species, eight in ten were changed by our noise.

scenes.label: Back to 2am
scenes.say: So the next time you hear a robin singing at night, now you know why. It's not confused.
It's just waiting for us to be quiet. Which animal surprised you the most? Tell me in the comments.

short.title: This Robin Sings at 2AM Because of You
short.description: Robins in noisy parts of Sheffield sing at night, when traffic finally stops (Fuller et al., Biology Letters 2007). Full countdown of 5 animals living with our noise on my channel.

scenes.say: Why is this robin singing at two in the morning? It's not lost.
Robins sing to guard their patch. If rivals can't hear them, they invade. But in the city, daytime traffic drowns the song out.
Scientists checked 121 spots across Sheffield, once by day and once at night.
The robins singing at night lived in the places that were loudest during the day.
Everyone blamed the street lights. Wrong. The daytime noise mattered much more than the light.
Night was about eight decibels quieter. That's the robin's window.
So it waits for the cars to stop, then sings. And that's why, at two in the morning, this robin is singing.
